sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Early Sepsis Management after Dog Bite
sections.description: Covers the patient’s initial presentation following a dog bite, early recognition of Capnocytophaga sepsis with DIC and multiorgan involvement, and first-line management decisions while cultures were pending.
subtopics: Dog bite exposure history and failure to start outpatient penicillin
Capnocytophaga canimorsus: reservoir, transmission, virulence, and clinical spectrum
Initial clinical findings: fever, hypoglycaemia, mottled extremities, pancytopenia, AKI, liver enzyme elevation, lactic acidosis
Recognition and scoring of sepsis and DIC; exclusion of necrotising fasciitis
Rationale for empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin/tazobactam) targeting dog-associated pathogens
Diagnostic delays with slow-growing organisms; blood culture confirmation timeline
ICU course: anuria, septic cardiomyopathy, CRRT initiation, supportive transfusions and coagulation management

sections.section_title: Transition from Sepsis/DIC to Thrombotic Microangiopathy
sections.description: Describes the clinical inflection point where improving sepsis unmasked MAHA and persistent thrombocytopenia, the evaluation of haemolysis, and tissue diagnosis confirming TMA.
subtopics: Clinical change despite improving inflammatory markers: isolated haemoglobin drop without bleeding
Laboratory evidence of haemolysis: undetectable haptoglobin, rising LDH, stable-to-low platelets
Pitfall: positive DAT after penicillin/transfusions mimicking autoimmune haemolysis; steroid trial and non-response
Peripheral smear with 15%–20% schistocytes confirming MAHA
Kidney biopsy timing (platelet threshold) and findings: acute tubular necrosis, ischaemic glomeruli, fibrin thrombi, crescents; absence of immune deposits
Interpretation: superimposed TMA on resolving DIC as the driver of ongoing haemolysis and renal failure

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning and Differential Diagnosis of TMA
sections.description: Details the stepwise algorithm to distinguish TTP, STEC-HUS, sepsis/DIC-associated MAHA, and complement-mediated HUS, including test selection, timing, and limitations.
subtopics: Initial priorities in TMA: exclude TTP rapidly (clinical urgency and mortality risk)
Use of PLASMIC score (patient score 4/7: low probability) and confirmatory ADAMTS13 activity (43.5%) to rule out TTP
Evaluation for STEC-HUS: clinical prodrome, stool PCR; negative in this case
Role and limitations of complement studies: normal C3/C4 do not exclude CM-HUS; pathway assays and their interpretive caveats
Impact of interventions on testing: PEX and eculizumab effects on complement assays and timing of samples
Indications and yield of renal biopsy in AKI with suspected TMA
Synthesis: persistent MAHA, thrombocytopenia, dialysis-dependent AKI, biopsy-proven TMA, exclusion of TTP/STEC → CM-HUS diagnosis

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology: Complement-Mediated HUS and Infection Triggers
sections.description: Explains alternative pathway dysregulation, genetic predisposition, and how C. canimorsus infection can trigger CM-HUS, including the paradox of complement in host defense versus endothelial injury.
subtopics: Alternative complement pathway activation and regulation (factors H, I, B; CD46) and endothelial injury leading to TMA
Genetic contributions and incomplete penetrance; role of autoantibodies (anti–factor H)
Infectious triggers of CM-HUS: pregnancy/autoimmune/drugs contrasted with bacterial triggers
C. canimorsus–complement interactions: variable serum susceptibility; capsule-mediated partial resistance
Clinical paradox: complement required for pathogen clearance but can amplify endothelial damage in susceptible hosts
Interpreting this case: extended testing with normal regulators, negative anti–factor H antibodies, markedly reduced AH50 post-therapy consistent with treatment effect rather than baseline deficiency
Comparison with literature: prior case with factor B variant vs current infection-triggered CM-HUS without identifiable pathogenic variants

sections.section_title: Therapeutic Strategy, Outcomes, and Clinical Lessons
sections.description: Outlines immediate and definitive treatments, timing considerations for complement blockade during infection, prevention of infectious complications, clinical response, and take-home points for practice.
subtopics: Sepsis management: targeted de-escalation to ampicillin/penicillin after culture results; source control and supportive care
Renal support: transition from anuria to recovery of diuresis; ongoing monitoring of creatinine and fluid status
PEX as bridge therapy in undifferentiated TMA and limited role in CM-HUS; transient improvement vs definitive control
Eculizumab initiation: dosing (900 mg weekly ×4 induction; 1200 mg q2 weeks maintenance), earlier use associated with better renal outcomes
Infectious risk mitigation with complement blockade: vaccination (MenACWY, MenB), antibiotic prophylaxis when vaccines not given ≥2 weeks prior, timing after culture sterilisation
Monitoring response: platelet recovery, LDH normalisation, haemoglobin stabilisation, renal trajectory; criteria to consider taper/cessation
Outcome in this case: haematologic remission, partial renal recovery (creatinine ~175 μmol/L), dialysis independence

Practice pearls: consider CM-HUS when haemolysis emerges as sepsis improves; normal C3/C4 do not exclude CM-HUS; use rapid ADAMTS13 to triage; biopsy supports diagnosis; balance infection control with timely complement blockade
